Par un vendredi matin ensoleillé, nous n: On a sunny Friday morning, we make our way to Montréal’s Old Port to visit a brand-new space: the Librairie Maktaba Bookshop, which opened almost four months ago. We are going to meet Sundus Abdul Hadi, the founder of the shop, but also so much more… She welcomes us into a space that feels like an Eastern living room. To a backdrop of traditional music, comfortably settled in the “living room” of her bookshop, she tells us her story and everything the Maktaba bookshop represents in her life.
« Je m’appelle Sundus Abdul Hadi ; je su: “My name is Sundus Abdul Hadi; I’m a mother, an artist, a writer and, today, a bookshop owner,” she says with a smile. If there is one thing to remember about her, it’s that Sundus smiles constantly. Born in Abu Dhabi but raised in Montréal, she has by no means forgotten her Iraqi roots. “I was born in Abu Dhabi; my parents left Iraq in the 1970s and I came here in the 1990s. Even though I wasn’t born in Iraq and I’ve now been here for 30 winters, my connection to that country is still there. I have one foot here and one foot there, I’m of Iraqi origin and I’m very proud of that.” “I love Montréal and I’m very grateful to be here,” Sundus continues, before turning to her writing projects. She is indeed also a writer, the author of the illustrated children’s book Shams and of the book Take Care of Your Self. “All of my artistic or creative work has a personal origin and comes from a long period when I worked on myself and practised—that’s the source of my work. You have to prove yourself to yourself, set goals in the face of obstacles. The first obstacle is self-confidence. Can I do it? When will I be able to do it? You are both your own best supporter and your own harshest critic; you have to find the balance between the two,” she says with assurance and experience.
La famille occupe une place essentielle: Family holds an essential place in the Iraqi artist’s life because, although Sundus is a writer and an entrepreneur, she is above all an artist. It is an end in itself, she says. “In a lot of families, you’re told you have to be an engineer, a doctor or a lawyer. I come from a family of artists, art is our way of life, and that’s very rare, this source of identity. My family is my first support; it gives me a lot of self-confidence.” When we brought up the culture shock between the countries of the East and Montréal, the subject of family came back to the table: “The shock of coming here? There wasn’t any. Ever since I immigrated here—when I was 10, 11 years old—we’ve stuck together and supported each other, as a family.” The artistic side is therefore hereditary for Sundus, who describes her Maktaba bookshop as the logical next step in her artistic projects. She is grateful to be where she is today, sitting with us, talking about her bookshop as a “gift.” “In life, you go through hard times where you fight, trying to push forward, and at some point, when you succeed, you think back on those hard times and realize that you’ve grown and evolved. Those moments are the foundations of your present life, and that’s important. Forget what you don’t have and be proud of what you already have!” Sundus concludes proudly, looking at her own achievement—the bookshop—from the inside.

Sundus aime raconter des histoires depui: Sundus has loved telling stories since she was little. “What inspires me is the mix of storytelling and justice in the world, a world that is precisely full of injustice. My inspiration is my community, my Iraqi community.” The Librairie Maktaba Bookshop brings together all of the Iraqi artist’s interests. This space was a need. She was looking for a place that represented her identity, her art and, above all, her community all at once, and she found the ideal place in this bookshop. “We’re a bookshop, a carefully tended and safe space. My job is to create this space where we can bring and discover our books together. Without the community, we can’t exist and open a space like Maktaba; we complete each other.
Ils soutiennent mon travail, et moi, leu: They support my work, and I support their needs—it creates a beautiful exchange. That’s why it was necessary to provide a space, a place of knowledge and inspiration,” she confides between two customers. Sundus Abdul Hadi is aware of the visibility she can now have thanks to her bookshop, especially in a tourist area like the Old Port. Smiling broadly since the start of our conversation, the writer takes on a more serious tone when she speaks of her desire for justice: “I have the responsibility and the resources as an artist to change things. The responsibility to speak about it, because I’m tired of all this injustice, tired of all these stereotypes, like ‘Arabs are violent,’ for example… Every community has a great culture, a rich heritage, a lot of knowledge and wisdom, and we have to share them with the world. Montréal is a place where I can be myself, a wonderful place to be an independent artist with a lot of support from the community. Thanks to that support, I can succeed here.”
Il y a donc une communauté au centre du: So there is a community at the heart of the “Maktaba” project, but also a concern about representation. “There’s very little room for the representation of people of colour here. Representation you can count on one hand. That’s why I was motivated to open Maktaba, because there’s a real need in the community and in my life.” A life that has seen many independent artistic projects. In fact, the bookshop is her first permanent space in Montréal. A community need met in part thanks to Maktaba: “You can be yourself if you feel represented, and that means a lot. It’s a big achievement when I see people come in and feel represented. I’m enjoying this moment, and that’s where I am right now, with this space. I’m very grateful and I’m living this moment to the fullest,” she says, her smile back.
Son histoire, Sundus la raconte dans <em: Sundus tells her story in Take Care of Your Self, where one expression comes up often: being “deeply rooted.” “This expression is a concept, a way of talking about marginalization, colonialism and racism in my book. It’s an expression that evokes our heritage, our richness, and that cuts across all cultures,” she explains. The writer tells this story for herself and for her children, but her work is also “an offering” to her readers. “Writing is a very important way for me to express myself, and then to give that to my children in the future. I want to share all this information and have it serve my children, but also our communities, all of our communities connected by the same problems,” Sundus sums up, speaking of her book, which came out two years ago.
Son côté à la fois artistique et curieux: Her artistic and curious side has allowed her to tell her story in her works, including Take Care of Your Self, a book that speaks of trauma, healing, struggles and care. It took her no less than 10 years of effort, work and research to complete. “We’re always aiming for the same thing! Whether it’s out of a concern for representation or identity, culture is the source of our work. Tell your own story! Whatever project you want to carry out, start by telling your own story and, with your heart, set yourself a goal and reach it. ‘When there’s a will, there’s a way,’ as they say in English—as long as you want something, you’ll always find a way to get there.” In her view, the idea is to know why it’s important to tell your story and how to do it. “The intention is to write, to share and to tell your own story,” she sums up passionately.
Dans un contexte de réélection provincia: In the context of the provincial re-election, with CAQ leader François Legault having said that welcoming more than 50,000 immigrants would be “suicidal,” the concern for representation is an integral part of Sundus’s story. She observes that here in Quebec, as in Canada, and more broadly in North America, the representation of immigrant communities is in a complicated situation. “I grew up at a time when Iraq was at war with the United States. There was war on Iraqi territory, but also in the media: the representation of the war in Iraq, and of Muslims especially, after the events of 9/11 led to a lot of brutality and racism toward people of colour. There’s a major problem of representation between real stories and realities and the way those stories are told or represented in the media, in books, in schools,” explains Sundus, reaffirming the importance of opening a bookshop for everyone, here in Montréal.
À travers son histoire, ses expériences: Through her story, her experiences and the Maktaba bookshop, Iraqi artist Sundus Abdul Hadi wants to pass on the power of knowledge to future generations and artists: “Knowledge also comes through books. So come pick up a book that could change your life!”
